shot.narration: 10,000 people, with homes, schools, a clinic, parks, and streets to walk along. And not one of them is standing on land.
shot.visual_purpose: The finished illustrative district in its bay; the camera passes over a cluster with two schools and three gardens on the lagoon, settles on one garden (lawn, trees, seats, play, the waterside promenade) for about two seconds, and goes low to the water's edge: the platform's side at the waterline; NOTE 'Illustrative design' [SEQUENCE 1/1: 4 view(s), 1 timed steps on floating_district: highlight 6]

shot.narration: Could we design a city like this, one that floats, stays where we put it, and keeps working? Let's treat it as a design problem, and solve it one step at a time.
shot.visual_purpose: From the water's edge the camera pulls back to the whole district during the question; at 'Let's treat it as a design problem' it comes down onto one home platform near the front, the one B04 strips down to, framed close among its neighbours, and the platform glows once at 'one step at a time'; no claim on screen [SEQUENCE 1/1: 3 view(s), 1 timed steps on floating_district: highlight 6]

elements.text: built · 46 households · a little over 100 people

shot.narration: Floating neighborhoods are not science fiction. In Amsterdam, a floating neighborhood called Schoonschip is home to 46 households, a little over 100 people. Much larger designs exist on paper. One, for 12,000 people off the coast of Busan in South Korea, was unveiled in 2022, and when we checked in November 2026, its architects still listed it as in design.
shot.visual_purpose: Scale card: Schoonschip (built, 46 households, schematic squares, no photograph) beside OCEANIX Busan (proposed 2022, three linked platforms, schematic); 'Architects' project page, Nov 2026: In Design' [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (57 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (57 elements)

shot.narration: So let's take our city apart, and build it back, one problem at a time.

shot.narration: Problem one: how does something this heavy float at all? Take a block of concrete. As a solid lump, it sinks: concrete is more than twice as dense as seawater. Shape the same concrete into a hollow box, 40 meters on each side, and it floats.
shot.visual_purpose: Section: a block holding the hull's concrete appears at the surface and sinks to the seabed; the same concrete as a hollow 40 m box then settles at its calculated draft (hull only) [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 7 timed steps on clay_boat: move 2, fade_out 2, fade_out 17, fade_in 2, move 2, reveal 17, highlight 17]

shot.narration: It floats because it pushes water out of the way, and the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the platform. Every ton we add needs roughly one more cubic meter of water pushed aside.

shot.narration: Real floating homes work exactly this way. The Schoonschip houses stand on concrete floats. The heaviest weighs around 340 to 350 metric tons, so it pushes aside roughly as many cubic meters of canal water: a cube about 7 meters on each side.
shot.visual_purpose: Schematic section of a floating home on its concrete float; '340–350 t'; the water it pushes aside as a cube about 7 m on each side, two 1.8 m figures for scale [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (15 elements)]

shot.narration: Our first platform, in this illustrative design, carries four blocks of three-story homes. Altogether it weighs about 4,800 tons, and floats about 3 meters deep. And here's the surprise: more than half of that weight is the concrete hull itself.

shot.narration: One fix is to make the hull half a meter deeper. That adds about 100 tons of concrete, 4% more, and brings the freeboard back to about a meter and 15 centimeters. Lighter buildings would be another way.
shot.visual_purpose: Two framings only, the camera still while anything changes: the east half of the section from deck to bottom while the bottom moves down 0.5 m and the walls and bulkheads grow with it (gold; the old bottom dashed for a while); then close on the waterline while the platform floats up to a freeboard of 1.15 m (the previous deck level dashed) [SEQUENCE 1/1: 3 view(s), 8 timed steps on floating_platform_section: move 90, fade_out 50, fade_in 1, move 3, reveal 11, fade_out 1, fade_in 1, move 88]

shot.narration: Will it tip over? Move 100 tons out toward the edge, and in this example the platform tilts by less than half a degree. But a small tilt under a shifted load tells us very little about how it will move in waves. Floating is only the first problem.
shot.visual_purpose: The same platform whole (four storeys, deeper hull), seen square on: the front buildings are taken away (inner roof caps first, so nothing shows through); a dashed level line and the deck's outline stay put; a 100 t block slides 15 m along a drawn arrow toward the edge, and the platform tilts by the angle calculated for this state (true scale) [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 9 timed steps on floating_platform_story: move 1, move 65, fade_out 24, fade_out 6, fade_out 18, fade_in 1, fade_in 1, move 1, rotate 66]

shot.narration: Let's go back to the three-story version. A platform like this holds about 50 people. For 10,000, we need a lot of them. So why not simply join them all into one enormous slab?

shot.narration: Look at two identical platforms carrying different buildings, one with two stories and one with four. Floating on their own, their decks would sit about 66 centimeters apart in height. So different loads add a demand on whatever connects them. In this design, the walkways between platforms are hinged, so they can follow the difference. Adding ballast to even out the decks would be another option.
shot.visual_purpose: Side elevation of two identical platforms with two and four storeys at their own drafts; close on the 0.66 m step between the decks; a hinged walkway arrives and spans it (no part shown failing) [SEQUENCE 1/1: 2 view(s), 5 timed steps on floating_pair: fade_out 3, highlight 2, highlight 2, reveal 3, highlight 2]

shot.narration: Connections are where engineers expect trouble. A 2026 research agenda lists stress concentrations on connectors among the challenges of large floating developments. One concept study links its modules flexibly, and spaces them far enough apart not to collide, because on flexible moorings they are expected to move sideways quite a lot.
shot.visual_purpose: Close-up of one joint: the gap, the hinged walkway, the flexible utility link and the fenders, each lit as it is named (conceptual geometry, not sized) [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 5 timed steps on neighbourhood_both_moorings: fade_out 20, highlight 6, highlight 2, highlight 1, highlight 2]

shots.explanation: 1 view(s), 5 timed steps on neighbourhood_both_moorings: fade_out 20, highlight 6, highlight 2, highlight 1, highlight 2

shot.narration: How many platforms would 10,000 people need? Say each resident needs about 40 square meters of floor: thirty for their home, and ten for a share of schools, shops and services. That's about thirty-three hectares of platform: about 200 platforms like our first one, with hundreds of connections between them.
shot.visual_purpose: One plan diagram (continues into B16): 40 m cells appear until about 33 ha are covered (209 cells); the joints between them light up as they are counted [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (244 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (244 elements)

elements.text: Schoonschip's floats: cast on the quay,
too big for houseboat dry docks

shot.narration: Bigger platforms mean fewer connections. At 100 meters on a side, 34 would do, but each would weigh about 30,000 tons, to build, launch and tow. Even the Schoonschip floats were too big for the dry docks of traditional houseboat builders, and were cast on the quay instead. Our district uses 60-meter platforms with three-story homes, 93 of them: a middle choice for this illustration, not an optimum.
shot.visual_purpose: Same diagram as B15: the cells regroup into 34 platforms of 100 m (fewer joints; about 30,000 t each), the Schoonschip quay note, then settle on the district's 93 platforms of 60 m around their lagoon [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (411 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (411 elements)

shot.narration: And all of this sits on water that never keeps still. Each platform rises and falls on its own, and every gap and hinge between them has to cope.

shot.narration: People living on the water feel it. Floating homes in the Netherlands can rock in storms, or when large cruise ships pass, and one Amsterdam resident feels it most on her upper floor.

elements.text: How exactly? An open research problem

shot.narration: Very large platforms don't only move. They bend, and predicting exactly how is still an open research problem.
shot.visual_purpose: A long platform drawn flat, then bending (exaggerated, conceptual); 'an open research problem' [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (29 elements)]

elements.text: our city: sheltered, connected to the shore

shot.narration: So the first fix is where you build. A 2026 concept study looks for sea areas with limited fetch, near a gulf, a strait or an archipelago, where waves stay moderate. That's why our city sits in a sheltered bay, connected to an existing city on shore.
shot.visual_purpose: Two schematic coasts: open coast with long fetch vs a sheltered bay with limited fetch; the district placed in the bay beside the city's quay [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (102 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (102 elements)

shot.narration: The second fix is the layout. Following one concept study, homes go in the middle, and functions that can tolerate more motion form the outer ring. Where the bay opens to the sea, a breakwater reduces the waves. But a floating breakwater may not be enough against longer waves from the open sea, and how much wave energy passes behind one is still hard to predict.
shot.visual_purpose: From the plan to an aerial view: inner homes light, then the outer ring of services; the breakwater arrives on the open side; NOTE 'reduces waves, does not remove storm risk' [SEQUENCE 1/1: 2 view(s), 5 timed steps on floating_district: fade_out 13, highlight 144, highlight 42, reveal 13, highlight 13]

shot.narration: Something also has to hold the city in place. Floating homes in the Netherlands are fixed to the shore, often resting against steel poles.
shot.visual_purpose: Low view of the neighbourhood: the water turns see-through (half its colour and the waterline stay) and the steel piles beneath light up [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 3 timed steps on neighbourhood_both_moorings: fade_out 20, ghost 1, highlight 20]

25 m bridge: slope changes ≈ 2.8° either way
shore hinge at the middle of the range

shot.narration: Water levels rise and fall, and a floating platform rises and falls with them, sliding along its poles. In our scenario, the water level can change by about 2 meters, so the bridges to shore need hinges: including changes in loading, the slope of a 25-meter bridge changes by about 3 degrees either way.
shot.visual_purpose: Elevation at true slope: quay, shore hinge, a 25 m link-span to a platform on its pile; the water and the platform rise and fall, the bridge turns on its hinge; '2 m water level (assumed) + loading; about 2.8° either way' [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (22 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (22 elements)

shot.narration: Further out, the water is deeper, and piles give way to mooring lines anchored in the seabed. Deeper water means longer lines, deeper anchors, and higher costs. The seabed itself shapes the design, and the bill.
shot.visual_purpose: Same neighbourhood; the water turns see-through (half its colour stays): the piles fade and mooring lines to anchors on the seabed take their place; lines and anchors light (conceptual mooring, not sized) [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 6 timed steps on neighbourhood_both_moorings: fade_out 20, ghost 1, fade_out 20, reveal 20, highlight 10, highlight 10]

shot.narration: So it floats, and it stays put. But is it a city yet? Fade out the buildings, and the city's other half appears.
shot.visual_purpose: Close to the quay: the buildings ghost and the city's other half appears: power, water and wastewater lines along the bridges and through the district [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 4 timed steps on floating_district: fade_out 18, ghost 312, fade_in 18, highlight 18]

shot.narration: Power first: at Schoonschip, 46 households share a single connection to the national grid, with solar panels, a battery in every house, and a smart grid between them. Floating doesn't mean off-grid.
shot.visual_purpose: Schematic: 46 homes on the water, one cable to the grid on land; solar panels, a battery per house, a smart grid between them; 'Floating ≠ off-grid' [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (164 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (164 elements)

shot.narration: Wastewater is separated there too: gray water from showers and washing machines, black water from toilets. Connecting floating homes to sewers on land takes extra infrastructure, such as waterproof cables and pumps. In our city, wastewater is pumped ashore along the bridges, and drinking water comes back the same way.
shot.visual_purpose: One bridge to the quay, close: the bridge deck ghosts, and the wastewater line beneath it, then the drinking-water line, light as they are named [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 4 timed steps on floating_district: highlight 1, ghost 1, highlight 1, highlight 1]

shot.narration: Transport, fire and medical services, and food all follow the same logic. A large floating development has to connect sewage, power and roads to land, or develop alternatives of its own, and our city connects.
shot.visual_purpose: The whole district: boat landings for fire and rescue, the emergency routes to the bridges, the utility lines, then the bridges themselves light in turn [SEQUENCE 1/1: 1 view(s), 4 timed steps on floating_district: highlight 2, highlight 3, highlight 18, highlight 3]

shot.narration: And if we also asked the city to supply itself, as one 2026 offshore concept does, it would need its own systems for energy, water and food. In that study, growing food alone accounts for nearly half of the city's estimated energy use.

shot.narration: And who gets to use the water? How districts like this fit into planning law is not yet known, and researchers warn they could end up serving the wealthy, and fencing off water that used to be public.
shot.visual_purpose: Two waterfront edges: a public path along the water vs a private, fenced edge; 'planning law: not yet known' [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (30 elements)]

elements.text: No reliable cost estimate for this design yet
the one published framework: preliminary; flotation and energy only

shot.narration: And what would it cost? We do not yet have a reliable cost estimate for this design. The one published framework we found is preliminary, and covers only flotation and energy. Compared with land, floating structures can follow the water level, and can be moved or reused, but they trade a fixed foundation for moorings, connections and ongoing maintenance.
shot.visual_purpose: Two columns, no numbers: what floating gives (follows the water, movable) and what it costs (moorings, connections, maintenance); 'no reliable cost estimate for this design yet' [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)]

elements.text: Could we build an entire city that floats?
Small floating neighbourhoods, sheltered and connected
A connected district for 10,000 in a sheltered bay
The one project of that size we checked: still listed as in design

shot.narration: A connected district for 10,000 people, in a sheltered bay, built step by step, may be possible under the right conditions. But how very large platforms bend, how their connections hold up, and what they would cost are still open questions. And the one project of that size we checked is still listed as in design.

coverage.narration: 10,000 people, with homes, schools, a clinic, parks, and streets to walk along. And not one of them is standing on land.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Could we design a city like this, one that floats, stays where we put it, and keeps working? Let's treat it as a design problem, and solve it one step at a time.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Floating neighborhoods are not science fiction. In Amsterdam, a floating neighborhood called Schoonschip is home to 46 households, a little over 100 people. Much larger designs exist on paper. One, for 12,000 people off the coast of Busan in South Korea, was unveiled in 2022, and when we checked in November 2026, its architects still listed it as in design.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: So let's take our city apart, and build it back, one problem at a time.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Problem one: how does something this heavy float at all? Take a block of concrete. As a solid lump, it sinks: concrete is more than twice as dense as seawater. Shape the same concrete into a hollow box, 40 meters on each side, and it floats.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: It floats because it pushes water out of the way, and the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the platform. Every ton we add needs roughly one more cubic meter of water pushed aside.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Real floating homes work exactly this way. The Schoonschip houses stand on concrete floats. The heaviest weighs around 340 to 350 metric tons, so it pushes aside roughly as many cubic meters of canal water: a cube about 7 meters on each side.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: Our first platform, in this illustrative design, carries four blocks of three-story homes. Altogether it weighs about 4,800 tons, and floats about 3 meters deep. And here's the surprise: more than half of that weight is the concrete hull itself.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Now add a fourth story. The platform settles about a third of a meter deeper, and the freeboard, the part of the hull above the water, shrinks from about a meter to about 70 centimeters.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: One fix is to make the hull half a meter deeper. That adds about 100 tons of concrete, 4% more, and brings the freeboard back to about a meter and 15 centimeters. Lighter buildings would be another way.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Will it tip over? Move 100 tons out toward the edge, and in this example the platform tilts by less than half a degree. But a small tilt under a shifted load tells us very little about how it will move in waves. Floating is only the first problem.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Let's go back to the three-story version. A platform like this holds about 50 people. For 10,000, we need a lot of them. So why not simply join them all into one enormous slab?
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Look at two identical platforms carrying different buildings, one with two stories and one with four. Floating on their own, their decks would sit about 66 centimeters apart in height. So different loads add a demand on whatever connects them. In this design, the walkways between platforms are hinged, so they can follow the difference. Adding ballast to even out the decks would be another option.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Connections are where engineers expect trouble. A 2026 research agenda lists stress concentrations on connectors among the challenges of large floating developments. One concept study links its modules flexibly, and spaces them far enough apart not to collide, because on flexible moorings they are expected to move sideways quite a lot.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: How many platforms would 10,000 people need? Say each resident needs about 40 square meters of floor: thirty for their home, and ten for a share of schools, shops and services. That's about thirty-three hectares of platform: about 200 platforms like our first one, with hundreds of connections between them.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: Bigger platforms mean fewer connections. At 100 meters on a side, 34 would do, but each would weigh about 30,000 tons, to build, launch and tow. Even the Schoonschip floats were too big for the dry docks of traditional houseboat builders, and were cast on the quay instead. Our district uses 60-meter platforms with three-story homes, 93 of them: a middle choice for this illustration, not an optimum.
issues: intent cross-check: declared COMPARE_VARIANTS, narration cues suggest ['EXPLAIN_DESIGN_CHANGE']
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: And all of this sits on water that never keeps still. Each platform rises and falls on its own, and every gap and hinge between them has to cope.
issues: intent cross-check: declared EXPLAIN_CAUSE_EFFECT, narration cues suggest ['SHOW_CONTEXT']
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: People living on the water feel it. Floating homes in the Netherlands can rock in storms, or when large cruise ships pass, and one Amsterdam resident feels it most on her upper floor.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: Very large platforms don't only move. They bend, and predicting exactly how is still an open research problem.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: So the first fix is where you build. A 2026 concept study looks for sea areas with limited fetch, near a gulf, a strait or an archipelago, where waves stay moderate. That's why our city sits in a sheltered bay, connected to an existing city on shore.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: The second fix is the layout. Following one concept study, homes go in the middle, and functions that can tolerate more motion form the outer ring. Where the bay opens to the sea, a breakwater reduces the waves. But a floating breakwater may not be enough against longer waves from the open sea, and how much wave energy passes behind one is still hard to predict.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Something also has to hold the city in place. Floating homes in the Netherlands are fixed to the shore, often resting against steel poles.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Water levels rise and fall, and a floating platform rises and falls with them, sliding along its poles. In our scenario, the water level can change by about 2 meters, so the bridges to shore need hinges: including changes in loading, the slope of a 25-meter bridge changes by about 3 degrees either way.
issues: intent cross-check: declared EXPLAIN_CAUSE_EFFECT, narration cues suggest ['EXPLAIN_DESIGN_CHANGE']
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: Further out, the water is deeper, and piles give way to mooring lines anchored in the seabed. Deeper water means longer lines, deeper anchors, and higher costs. The seabed itself shapes the design, and the bill.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: So it floats, and it stays put. But is it a city yet? Fade out the buildings, and the city's other half appears.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Power first: at Schoonschip, 46 households share a single connection to the national grid, with solar panels, a battery in every house, and a smart grid between them. Floating doesn't mean off-grid.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: Wastewater is separated there too: gray water from showers and washing machines, black water from toilets. Connecting floating homes to sewers on land takes extra infrastructure, such as waterproof cables and pumps. In our city, wastewater is pumped ashore along the bridges, and drinking water comes back the same way.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Transport, fire and medical services, and food all follow the same logic. A large floating development has to connect sewage, power and roads to land, or develop alternatives of its own, and our city connects.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Everything so far assumed sheltered water close to a city. So what happens if we tow it out to sea?
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Longer waves arrive, and a floating breakwater may not be enough against them. Below the surface, the seabed drops away, so mooring lines get longer and anchors deeper.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Further from shore, cables, pipes and supply ships can still reach the city, but every link becomes longer and more exposed.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: And if we also asked the city to supply itself, as one 2026 offshore concept does, it would need its own systems for energy, water and food. In that study, growing food alone accounts for nearly half of the city's estimated energy use.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: That study also uses a different kind of hull: semi-submersible platforms, with the deck raised above the sea on columns, behind a floating barrier. Offshore isn't the same city moved further out. It's a different design.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Some difficulties remain wherever we build. Concrete in seawater needs watching: chlorides can corrode the steel reinforcement, and, according to a 2026 study, there are no dedicated standards for floating cities yet.
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: Large floating developments change the light, shade and water movement beneath them, effects that researchers say still need study, and they expect the impact on local ecology to be far larger than that of small developments.
issues: intent cross-check: declared SHOW_CONTEXT, narration cues suggest ['EXPLAIN_DESIGN_CHANGE']
explanation: SEQUENCE: One model, steps timed to the narration: the camera eases from one framing to the next (same preset), parts ghost, fade out, arrive and glow in turn (beat 'sequence')

coverage.narration: And who gets to use the water? How districts like this fit into planning law is not yet known, and researchers warn they could end up serving the wealthy, and fencing off water that used to be public.
explanation: CARD: 2D card (text/arrows) supplied by the beat

coverage.narration: And what would it cost? We do not yet have a reliable cost estimate for this design. The one published framework we found is preliminary, and covers only flotation and energy. Compared with land, floating structures can follow the water level, and can be moved or reused, but they trade a fixed foundation for moorings, connections and ongoing maintenance.
